title: The psychological benefits of indoor plants: A critical review of the experimental literature

findings.consequent: General psychological benefits (e.g., stress-reduction, pain tolerance)
findings.quote: The reviewed studies suggest that indoor plants can provide psychological benefits such as stress-reduction and increased pain tolerance. However, they also showed substantial heterogeneity in methods and results. We therefore have strong reservations about general claims that indoor plants cause beneficial psychological changes.
Some findings recur, notably enhanced pain management with plants... All four of the studies found that those with plants present had better tolerance for pain than those without plants present.

findings.consequent: Stress reduction, pain tolerance, perceived room attractiveness
findings.quote: several of the studies suggest that flowering plants have a greater effect compared to foliage plants, as seen in stress-reduction (Kim & Mattson, 2002), pain tolerance (Park et al., 2004), and perceived attractiveness of the room (Adachi, Rohde, & Kendle, 2000).

Shibata and Suzuki (2001) considered circumstances under which plants would affect task-performance through effects on attention. Their results were in line with the hypothesis that plants would more effectively reduce attentional fatigue during a break from work than while performing a task because people could allow their attention to go to the plants during a break.

findings.consequent: Creative task performance (increase) vs. attentionally demanding task performance (decrease)
findings.quote: In a later study, Shibata and Suzuki (2002) hypothesized that plants would facilitate performance on a creative task because they are a source of information, but that they would distract a person working on a more attentionally demanding task. Their participants performed better on an association task compared to a more attentionally demanding task when they had a plant placed in front of them, compared to a no-plant condition. However, this held only for their male subjects.

Similarly, Larsen et al. (1998) found that perfor- mance on a letter identification task decreased with a larger number of plants, which agrees with the notion that fascinating properties of plants may interfere with some kinds of tasks.

Several of the studies did not find effects on emotions after the participants were exposed to plants... The results were also variable among the subset of studies that used Zuckerman's (1977) Inventory of Personal Reac- tions (ZIPERS). The studies either found significant differences only on an item-level... or they reported different results across gender.

The psychophysiological results are also mixed. Some findings are consistent with the theory (e.g., Lohr et al., 1996), and others are not (Lohr & Pearson-Mims, 2000). Kim and Mattson (2002) found decreased electrodermal activity and EEG beta activity (taken as indicators of stress recovery) with exposure to red-flowering geraniums versus geraniums without flowers and no plants.

findings.consequent: Perceived room attractiveness, cheerfulness, pleasantness, invitingness
findings.quote: The room with plants was also perceived as more cheerful, pleasant, and inviting than the room with the other aesthetic amenities.
